Acquired resistance significantly limits the long-term clinical benefit of osimertinib in EGFR-mutant lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD). However, the early non-genetic adaptations and microenvironmental crosstalk that enable initial tumor survival remain poorly defined. This study aimed to elucidate the epigenetic-immune mechanisms driving osimertinib resistance and to identify novel actionable therapeutic targets.

We integrated transcriptomic profiling and clinical cohort analyses to identify therapy-induced secreted factors during the evolution of EGFR-TKI resistance. The upstream regulatory mechanisms were characterized using ChIP, Co-IP, and dual-luciferase reporter assays. The dual functional roles of the identified factor, serum amyloid A1 (SAA1), in tumor-intrinsic signaling and macrophage polarization were investigated in vitro. Finally, the therapeutic efficacy of combining SAA1 neutralization with osimertinib was evaluated across patient-derived organoids, xenografts, and immunocompetent spontaneous lung tumor models.

We identified SAA1 as a critical therapy-induced secreted factor that progressively increases during the transition from drug tolerance to established resistance, which negatively correlates with clinical outcomes in patients receiving osimertinib. Mechanistically, osimertinib treatment suppressed the ERK-dependent phosphorylation of the transcriptional repressor GATAD2A at Ser114. This event destabilized the NuRD complex, thereby relieving the epigenetic transcriptional repression of SAA1. Secreted SAA1 promoted therapeutic resistance through dual mechanisms: activating the autocrine TLR4/NF-κB survival signaling in tumor cells and inducing the paracrine polarization of pro-tumorigenic SPP1⁺ macrophages. Therapeutically, targeted neutralization of SAA1 synergized robustly with osimertinib to reverse immunosuppressive remodeling and induce profound tumor regression in multiple preclinical models.

Our findings define a novel therapy-induced ERK/GATAD2A/SAA1 epigenetic-immune axis that drives acquired resistance to osimertinib. SAA1 acts as a pivotal bridge between tumor-intrinsic survival adaptations and microenvironmental immune suppression, highlighting SAA1 neutralization as a tractable combinatorial strategy to enhance EGFR-TKI efficacy in LUAD.

Lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD) remains the leading cause of cancer mortality worldwide [1, 2]. While osimertinib is the standard first-line therapy for EGFR-mutant LUAD, acquired resistance inevitably develops within 10–20 months [3–6]. This therapeutic failure is driven by drug-tolerant persister cells (DTPCs) and heterogeneous mechanisms, ranging from EGFR mutations (e.g., C797S) to extensive tumor microenvironment (TME) remodeling [7–10]. Given the limited efficacy of immune checkpoint blockade in this setting, identifying actionable targets to modulate TME-mediated resistance is urgently needed [11].

Secreted factors within the TME are central to acquired resistance. Drug-induced transcriptional reprogramming and TME-derived signals promote the release of cytokines, chemokines, and matrix-associated proteins that activate survival pathways, suppress apoptosis, and foster immune evasion [12, 13]. Although targeting secreted proteins has proven clinically effective in other contexts, the identity of secreted mediators specifically induced during EGFR-TKI treatment and their functional contribution to osimertinib resistance remain unclear [14, 15].

Here, we identify serum amyloid A1 (SAA1) as a key mediator of osimertinib resistance, robustly upregulated in EGFR-mutant LUAD upon treatment. Mechanistically, osimertinib inhibits ERK-dependent phosphorylation of GATAD2A at S114, relieving transcriptional repression of SAA1. Functionally, SAA1 drives resistance via dual mechanisms: autocrine NF-κB activation and paracrine polarization of pro-tumorigenic macrophages. Importantly, combining osimertinib with SAA1 neutralization yields potent therapeutic benefit across multiple in vivo models, providing a compelling rationale for targeting this axis to overcome acquired resistance.

To identify secreted mediators of osimertinib resistance, we subjected three EGFR-mutant LUAD cell lines (PC-9, HCC827, and H1975) to osimertinib at respective IC50 concentrations for 48 h (Fig. 1A). RNA-seq profiling revealed six differentially expressed genes that encode secreted proteins (MEGF6, SAA1, PNP, THBS3, ST6GALNAC2, and CFB). Among these candidates, SAA1 was prioritized due to its comparatively high basal abundance and robust transcriptional induction following osimertinib exposure (Fig. 1B). Despite its frequent identification as a potential biomarker, the functional significance of SAA1 in LUAD remains largely unexamined [16, 17].

Western blot and Enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) confirmed a dose-dependent increase in SAA1 secretion, with extracellular levels exceeding 10 ng/mL after 10 nM osimertinib exposure (Fig. 1C, D). To determine whether this induction tracked along the resistance continuum, we examined SAA1 expression in short-term drug-tolerant persister cells (DTPCs) (10 days; 200 nM for PC-9, 1 µM for H1975) and in long-term acquired osimertinib-resistant (OR) lines (stepwise dose escalation over three months) [18, 19]. Phenotypically, OR cells exhibited a > 20-fold increase in osimertinib IC50 and displayed broad cross-resistance to gefitinib, afatinib, and the fourth-generation inhibitor BDTX-1535 (Fig. 1E; Figure S1). Crucially, SAA1 expression exhibited a distinct, stepwise elevation transitioning from the DTPC state to established resistance, suggesting its pivotal role in sustaining the drug-tolerant phenotype (Fig. 1F, G).

Clinical samples mirrored these findings. Immunohistochemistry demonstrated marked SAA1 protein accumulation in EGFR-mutant LUAD tumors compared to normal tissues, with further enrichment observed in post-treatment residual samples (Fig. 1H). Analysis of five paired EGFR-mutant LUAD samples collected before and after neoadjuvant osimertinib showed increased SAA1 expression in post-treatment residual tumors. IHC H-score quantification demonstrated elevated SAA1 protein levels in TKI-residual samples (Fig. 1I), consistent with increased SAA1 mRNA and protein quantification (Figure S1E). Moreover, in a retrospective cohort of 40 patients receiving adjuvant osimertinib, high baseline SAA1 expression was significantly associated with inferior disease-free survival, conferring an increased risk of recurrence (HR = 2.59, p = 0.006) (Fig. 1K). Collectively, these multi-tiered data indicate that SAA1 is induced during osimertinib adaptation and resistance, and suggest that elevated baseline SAA1 expression may be associated with unfavorable outcomes in EGFR-mutant LUAD patients receiving adjuvant osimertinib.

To delineate the functional requirement of SAA1 in intrinsic resistance, we performed loss-of-function assays using two independent siRNAs. In parental cells, SAA1 knockdown sensitized cells to osimertinib, reducing the IC50 by approximately 3-fold and significantly suppressing proliferation rates (Fig. 2A, B; Supplementary Figure S2A, B).

We subsequently interrogated SAA1 function in established resistance using SAA1-overexpressing (SAA1-OE) and knockout (SAA1-KO) PC-9OR and H1975OR models (Fig. 2C). SAA1 overexpression conferred robust cross-resistance to EGFR-TKIs, whereas CRISPR/Cas9-mediated ablation of SAA1 restored drug sensitivity, which was fully reversible upon exogenous SAA1 supplementation (Fig. 2D, E). Colony formation and EdU assays corroborated that SAA1 is required for clonogenic survival and DNA synthesis under drug pressure (Supplementary Figure S2C-E). Crucially, Annexin V/PI flow cytometry revealed that SAA1 ablation induced massive apoptosis upon TKI treatment and can be rescued by exogenous SAA1 (Supplementary Figure S2F, G).

Given the progressive induction of SAA1 during initial treatment, we hypothesized it is essential for the survival of DTPCs. Supplementation with exogenous SAA1 significantly enhanced DTPC formation efficiency (Fig. 2F). Furthermore, long-term tracking demonstrated that SAA1 ablation profoundly delayed the emergence of DTPCs, whereas SAA1 overexpression accelerated acquired resistance (Supplementary Figure S2H).

Importantly, to clarify whether this dependency is strictly restricted to the resistant state, we evaluated SAA1-KO effects in parallel across parental and OR lines. While SAA1 ablation exerted a moderate growth-suppressive effect in parental cells, it triggered a drastically more profound proliferation blockade and heightened osimertinib sensitivity in OR cells (Supplementary Figure S2I, J).

Finally, we evaluated therapeutic efficacy in vivo using a PC-9OR CDX model. While osimertinib monotherapy yielded modest inhibition, combining SAA1 knockout with osimertinib induced potent tumor regression (~ 100 mm³ vs. ~300 mm³, p < 0.001) (Fig. 2G, H). Immunohistochemical analysis in the combination group confirmed not only a marked reduction in the Ki67 proliferation index but also a striking accumulation of cleaved caspase-3 positive cells, indicating profound in vivo apoptotic sensitization (Supplementary Figure S2K). Collectively, these data establish SAA1 as a critical anti-apoptotic driver of both the initial drug-tolerant state and established acquired resistance.

To elucidate the mechanism underlying SAA1-mediated resistance, we interrogated signaling pathways associated with high SAA1 expression. Analysis of TCGA-LUAD datasets revealed a significant enrichment of NF-κB signaling in SAA1-high tumors (Supplementary Figure S3A, B). Consistent with these clinical observations, RNA-seq profiling of PC-9 and H1975 cells treated with exogenous SAA1 demonstrated a robust, coordinated upregulation of multiple NF-κB-associated genes (Fig. 3A, B; Supplementary Figure S3C-E).

To rigorously validate this pathway activation across the evolution of resistance, we assessed the specific phosphorylation status and subcellular localization of the NF-κB p65 (RelA) subunit. Biochemically, both DTPCs and established OR lines displayed markedly elevated phosphorylation of p65 at the classical Serine 536 site (p-p65 S536), coupled with increased phosphorylation and acute degradation of IκBα, compared to their parental counterparts (Supplementary Figure S3F). This intense pathway activation was accompanied by profound nuclear translocation of p65 (Supplementary Figure S3G) and a synchronized transcriptional upregulation of canonical downstream targets, including NFKBIA, BCL2, CXCL8, and IL6 (Supplementary Figure S3H). Importantly, the hyperactivation of this axis was strictly dependent on SAA1. Genetic ablation (SAA1-KO) completely suppressed p-p65 activation and its nuclear accumulation, which was fully rescued by the addition of exogenous SAA1 (Fig. 3C, D; Supplementary Figure S3I).

Because SAA1 functions as a secreted factor, we sought to pinpoint the primary membrane receptor mediating this pro-survival signal. We evaluated TLR2 and TLR4, two prominent candidate receptors implicated in SAA1 signaling. While siRNA-mediated depletion of both receptors was highly efficient, the knockdown of TLR4 sensitized OR cells to osimertinib far more profoundly than TLR2 depletion (Supplementary Figure S4A-C). Subsequent biochemical validation confirmed that silencing TLR4 specifically and comprehensively abrogated SAA1-induced p65 phosphorylation, nuclear translocation, and downstream target gene transcription, firmly establishing TLR4 as the indispensable conduit for SAA1-driven NF-κB activation (Supplementary Figure S4D-G).

Finally, we evaluated the functional and phenotypic consequences of blocking this axis using specific pharmacological inhibitors against NF-κB (BAY 11-7082) or TLR4 (TAK-242). Both inhibitors effectively abolished SAA1-induced p-p65 (S536) activation and nuclear translocation (Fig. 3E-H). Crucially, addressing the classical role of NF-κB in conferring tumor survival, we demonstrated that while blocking this axis impaired cell proliferation to some extent, its paramount mechanism of action was governing apoptotic resistance (Fig. 3I-L). Flow cytometry assays revealed that SAA1 robustly shielded OR cells from osimertinib-induced apoptosis. However, targeted co-treatment with either NF-κB inhibitor or TLR4 inhibitor acutely dismantled this anti-apoptotic shield, fully resensitizing the resistant tumor cells to osimertinib-induced cell death (Supplementary Figure S4H, I). Together, these multidimensional data demonstrate that SAA1 strictly relies on the TLR4/NF-κB survival axis to confer osimertinib resistance.

Secreted proteins not only regulate tumor-intrinsic functions through autocrine signaling but, more importantly, orchestrate TME remodeling via paracrine interactions. SAA1 has previously been identified as a key factor in the invasive zone of liver cancer, where it recruits macrophages via FPR1/TLR receptors to drive M2-like polarization [20].

In xenograft tumors treated with osimertinib, we observed a marked accumulation of F4/80⁺CD206⁺ macrophages, a feature that was largely abolished when SAA1 was genetically depleted in tumor cells, as confirmed by rigorous quantitative analysis (Fig. 4A, B). This indicated that tumor-derived SAA1 actively recruits and programs macrophages during therapy. Furthermore, direct treatment with exogenous SAA1 was sufficient to drive M2 polarization, as evidenced by flow cytometry, which showed a significant expansion of the CD206⁺ population from ~ 30% in controls to ~ 50% in SAA1-treated groups (Fig. 4C, D; Figure S5A). To validate this paracrine crosstalk, we co-cultured established human (THP-1) and mouse (BMDM) macrophage models with OR cell lines. Consistent with the in vivo data, exposure to osimertinib-treated tumor cells induced a robust upregulation of classical M2 markers (CD206, VEGFA, TGFB1, IL-10, ARG1) in both macrophage types, with IL-10 showing a particularly strong induction. This polarization was strictly dependent on tumor-derived SAA1, as SAA1 knockout in the cancer cells significantly reversed marker expression to near-basal levels (Fig. 4E; Figure S5B).

Beyond the classical M1/M2 paradigm, SAA1 also induced strong expression of SPP1, a marker of pro-angiogenic, tumor-supportive macrophage subsets recently implicated in therapy resistance (Fig. 4F) [21]. Mechanistically, we sought to delineate the specific receptor dependency of this macrophage reprogramming. While pharmacological inhibition of TLR4 (TAK-242) partially attenuated the expression of M2 markers and the frequency of CD206⁺ macrophage, head-to-head comparisons revealed that inhibition of TLR2 (inhibited by C29) exerted a more profound suppressive effect (Fig. 4G-I; Figure S5C-E). Treatment with a TLR2 inhibitor nearly completely reversed the SAA1-induced upregulation of M2 markers and CD206⁺ polarization, identifying TLR2 as the predominant paracrine receptor mediating SAA1 signaling in macrophages (Fig. 4H-I; Figure S5C-E). Clinically, multiplex immunofluorescence analysis of the same five paired EGFR-mutant LUAD samples described in Fig. 1H–I further supported these findings. These samples were collected before and after neoadjuvant osimertinib treatment, with TKI-naïve specimens obtained from pre-treatment needle biopsies and TKI-residual specimens obtained from surgically resected residual tumors. Crucially, co-staining revealed that SPP1 was predominantly induced within the CD206⁺ compartment (Fig. 4L). Quantitative analysis demonstrated a striking increase in the proportion of SPP1⁺ cells among CD68⁺CD206⁺ macrophages in TKI-residual tissues compared to TKI-naïve baselines (Fig. 4J, K). These data demonstrate that osimertinib-induced SAA1 actively reshapes the immune microenvironment by driving classical M2 macrophages into a highly specialized, pro-tumorigenic SPP1⁺/CD206⁺ terminal state.

Gene expression can be regulated at multiple levels, including transcriptional control, translational regulation, and post-translational modifications [22–24]. Given the concordance between SAA1 mRNA and protein induction, we investigated transcriptional regulation of SAA1. DNA pull-down assays utilizing a biotinylated SAA1 promoter probe identified 41 candidates, which were refined to five potential regulators (RXRA, YY1, ETV6, MAX, and GATAD2A) by integrating GTRD ChIP-seq datasets (Fig. 5A; Table S6). Functional screening via siRNA-mediated knockdown revealed that only GATAD2A depletion resulted in a robust and reproducible upregulation of SAA1 expression, identifying it as a putative transcriptional repressor (Fig. 5B; Figure S6A-B). Validation in two cell lines confirmed that GATAD2A loss mimics and significantly amplifies osimertinib-induced SAA1 expression at both the transcript and protein levels (Fig. 5C, D; Figure S6C, D).

Mechanistically, ChIP-seq motif analysis identified a GATAD2A binding site near the SAA1 promoter, which was validated by ChIP-qPCR enrichment in PC-9 and H1975 cells (Figs. 5E-F). Functionally, GATAD2A knockdown increased wild-type SAA1 promoter activity, whereas mutation of the binding site abolished this derepression (Fig. 5G). These data conclusively demonstrate that GATAD2A functions as a direct transcriptional repressor of SAA1.

We next explored how osimertinib impairs GATAD2A function. Given that post-translational modifications are critical regulators of protein activity, and that EGFR-driven hyperactivation of downstream kinases (e.g., ERK and AKT) is tightly linked to aberrant phosphorylation events, we hypothesized that osimertinib might alter the phosphorylation state of GATAD2A, thereby disrupting its repressive function [25–28].

To identify specific regulatory sites, we performed label-free quantitative phosphoproteomics in PC-9 parental and OR cells. This profiling identified serine 114 (S114) as the most significantly hypophosphorylated residue in the resistant context (Fig. 5H). Bioinformatic analysis using Scansite 4 predicted that the S114 motif is a high-stringency substrate for ERK [29]. Western blot analysis confirmed that osimertinib or ERK inhibition (SCH772984) abolished GATAD2A phosphorylation at S114 without affecting total protein levels (Figure S6E).

Although S114 has been previously cataloged in mass spectrometry datasets, its functional role has remained uncharacterized [30, 31]. To define its role, we generated a phosphorylation-deficient GATAD2AS114A knock-in model using CRISPR/Cas9. These mutant cells exhibited constitutive SAA1 upregulation, phenocopying osimertinib treatment (Fig. 5I).

Mechanistically, since GATAD2A scaffolds the NuRD complex, we hypothesized S114 phosphorylation governs stability [32]. Co-IP and proximity ligation assays (PLA) revealed that osimertinib, ERK inhibition, or the S114A mutation disrupted GATAD2A interaction with core NuRD subunits (MBD2/MTA2) (Figs. 5J-L). Thus, osimertinib-mediated ERK inactivation leads to GATAD2A dephosphorylation, NuRD complex disassembly, and subsequent SAA1 derepression.

To assess the translational potential of targeting the SAA1 axis, we employed a neutralizing antibody (Anti-SAA1) validated for cross-reactivity against both human and mouse SAA1 [33]. Dose-titration assays in PC-9OR and H1975OR cells identified 1 µg/mL as the optimal saturating concentration, beyond which no additional inhibitory effect was observed (Figure S7A). At this concentration, Anti-SAA1 markedly suppressed cell proliferation, colony formation, and osimertinib resistance in OR cell lines (Fig. 6A; Figure S7B, C). Crucially, systemic Anti-SAA1 (0.25 µg/g) in C57BL/6 mice elicited no toxicity, with histopathology of major organs confirming a favorable safety profile (Figure S7D). To clarify whether this dependency is strictly restricted to the resistant state, we compared Anti-SAA1 monotherapy across parental and OR models. While SAA1 neutralization exerted a moderate suppressive effect on parental cells, it triggered a drastically more profound growth blockade in OR cells both in vitro (Figure S7E, F) and in CDX models (Figure S7G, H). This parallel comparison confirms that while SAA1 provides a baseline survival advantage, osimertinib-driven resistant cells become uniquely addicted to this induced survival axis.

We next evaluated therapeutic efficacy across multiple in vivo platforms. In PC-9OR CDX model, while monotherapy yielded partial inhibition, the combination of Anti-SAA1 and osimertinib induced overt tumor regression, reducing mean tumor volume to ~ 70 mm3 compared to ~ 220 mm3 in the osimertinib-only group (Fig. 6C, D). To functionally dissect whether this in vivo efficacy relies on autocrine tumor inhibition or macrophage modulation, we performed macrophage depletion using clodronate liposomes (Figure S7I). Notably, macrophage depletion significantly attenuated the combinatorial efficacy of Anti-SAA1 and osimertinib (Figure S7J), proving that the full therapeutic benefit requires the presence of macrophages, even in an immunodeficient setting. This efficacy was strictly recapitulated in PDOs and PDX. In PDO models, combination treatment disrupted organoid architecture and significantly reduced ATP-based viability. Similarly, in PDX models derived from resistant patients, the combination regimen achieved superior tumor growth control compared to either single agent (Fig. 6E-G; Figure S7K).

Given the dual impact of SAA1 on both tumor cells and macrophages, we further utilized an immunocompetent genetically engineered mouse model (GEMM) harboring the EGFRL858R/T790M mutations (hEGFRL858R/T790M). Lung tumors were induced by intratracheal delivery of AAV encoding lung-epithelial-specific Cre recombinase (Scgb1a1-Cre) in 8-week-old mice (Fig. 6H). Following a 30-day latency for tumor development, mice were randomized to treatment arms. Longitudinal micro-CT imaging revealed that the combination of osimertinib and Anti-SAA1 markedly suppressed tumor burden compared to monotherapy after 4-week evaluation from the start of treatment (Fig. 6I). Most significantly, this regimen conferred a robust survival advantage, extending the median survival from 105.5 days in the osimertinib-treated group to 149.5 days in the combination group (log-rank p < 0.001) (Fig. 6J). These results demonstrate that SAA1 neutralization overcomes resistance in both immunodeficient and immunocompetent settings, underscoring its translational relevance.

To elucidate whether this in vivo efficacy is driven by tumor-intrinsic inhibition or microenvironmental remodeling, we profiled the GEMM tumor tissues. Immunohistochemistry confirmed that anti-SAA1 abrogated tumor-intrinsic NF-κB signaling, which translated to robust proliferative arrest and massive apoptosis (Fig. 6K). Concurrently, multiplex immunofluorescence revealed profound immune reprogramming. While osimertinib monotherapy enriched the immunosuppressive SPP1+CD206+ M2 macrophage population, SAA1 neutralization significantly reduced this subpopulation and increased CD8+ T cell infiltration (Fig. 6K-L). Collectively, SAA1 neutralization overcomes resistance through a dual mechanism: promoting tumor cell apoptosis and reversing M2-mediated immunosuppression.

Acquired resistance remains the overarching challenge in the clinical management of EGFR-mutant LUAD, fundamentally limiting the long-term benefit of third-generation TKIs like osimertinib [7, 9, 34]. While late-stage resistance is often attributed to genomic alterations, the early non-genetic adaptations that permit tumor cell survival under drug pressure are poorly defined. Here, we identify a mechanism of therapy-induced secretome remodeling that links initial drug tolerance to stable resistance. We show that SAA1 is not merely an inflammatory bystander but a central orchestrator of the resistant state, coordinating tumor-intrinsic survival signaling with tumor microenvironment reprogramming.

A key conceptual advance of our work is the positioning of SAA1 as an evolutionary bridge connecting initial drug tolerance to stable resistance. SAA1 is classically characterized as an acute-phase reactant synthesized by the liver during systemic inflammation [35]. However, we demonstrate that in the context of TKI therapy, it acts as an autocrine “SOS signal”. This signal is transduced via the TLR4/NF-κB axis. The NF-κB pathway is a master regulator of anti-apoptotic signaling and has been widely implicated in resistance to chemotherapy and targeted agents [36–38]. By activating this pathway, SAA1 elevates the apoptotic threshold, allowing DTPC to survive the initial therapeutic bottleneck. This finding mirrors observations in head and neck squamous cell carcinoma, where NF-κB activation blunts the efficacy of EGFR inhibitors [39]. Importantly, this mechanism operates independently of genomic change, highlighting how adaptive transcriptional programs sustain early survival under kinase inhibition.

Beyond intrinsic survival, SAA1 fundamentally reshapes the TME. Recent studies reveal that EGFR inhibition triggers extensive surfaceome remodeling, exposing new therapeutic vulnerabilities [40]. Complementing these findings, our work highlights that the secreted signaling network is equally dynamic and critical for orchestrating immune evasion. We identify SPP1⁺ macrophages as the dominant effector subset induced by SAA1. Unlike classical M2 macrophages, SPP1⁺ TAMs represent a specialized, pro-angiogenic, and fibrotic population associated with poor immunotherapy outcomes [41, 42]. Importantly, we demonstrate that this SAA1-driven accumulation of SPP1⁺ macrophages creates a physical and functional barrier that spatially excludes cytotoxic CD8⁺ T cells. Notably, we highlight a fascinating cell-type-specific receptor compartmentalization: while SAA1 primarily engages TLR4 to drive tumor-intrinsic survival, it orchestrates the recruitment and polarization of macrophages predominantly via a TLR2-dependent paracrine mechanism. Our macrophage depletion studies (in vivo clodronate liposome assays) unequivocally confirm that this paracrine axis is functionally indispensable for resistant phenotype. We also provide evidence that SAA1 recruits and polarizes macrophages via a TLR4-dependent paracrine mechanism, which expands the concept of therapy adaptation from tumor cell autonomy to the coordinated remodeling of the surrounding immune ecosystem [43–45]. This aligns with spatial transcriptomic findings in liver cancer, where SAA1 dictates macrophage recruitment at the invasive front [20]. This finding expands the concept of therapy adaptation from tumor cell autonomy to coordinated remodeling of the surrounding immune ecosystem.

Mechanistically, we uncover a “therapy paradox” linking kinase inhibition to transcriptional derepression: the pharmacological inhibition of EGFR/ERK—intended to kill the tumor—inadvertently disrupts the epigenetic machinery governing cell identity. Notably, the regulatory serine 114 of GATAD2A resides within a predicted intrinsically disordered region, a structural feature frequently associated with protein–protein interactions [46, 47]. Our data indicate that the loss of ERK-dependent phosphorylation at this site coincides with a compromised interaction between GATAD2A and the NuRD complex core subunits. This destabilization relieves transcriptional repression at the SAA1 promoter, unleashing its expression [48]. This mechanism illustrates how targeted therapies can inadvertently induce epigenetic instability, permitting stress-responsive gene programs to emerge as adaptive survival strategies.

The dual role of SAA1 makes it an ideal target for combination therapy. Combining a neutralizing SAA1 antibody with osimertinib induced robust tumor regression across multiple preclinical models, including CDX, PDO, PDX, and, most importantly, an immunocompetent spontaneous lung tumor model [33, 49]. This finding is clinically significant as it confirms efficacy in a native immune microenvironment, a limitation of traditional immunodeficient xenografts. This provides a mechanistic rationale for deploying anti-SAA1 strategies to overcome the immunosuppressive “cold” TME characteristic of EGFR-mutant tumors, offering a promising translational avenue to extend the durability of third-generation EGFR-TKIs.

Our study has several limitations. First, while clinical correlations were established, our analysis relied primarily on baseline resected tumors; longitudinal paired biopsies are needed to definitively track SAA1 dynamics during therapy progression. Second, although we identified the TLR4/NF-κB axis and macrophage polarization as key drivers, the potential involvement of alternative receptors (e.g., FPR1) and the complex spatial heterogeneity of the immune microenvironment warrant further characterization using spatial and single-cell transcriptomics. Finally, the broader applicability of the GATAD2A-NuRD regulatory mechanism to other generations of EGFR-TKIs and different cancer contexts remains to be explored in future studies.

Collectively, our findings define an EGFR–GATAD2A–SAA1–TLR4 axis as a central driver of non-genetic resistance. By targeting both the oncogenic driver and the therapy-induced secretome, this dual strategy may extend the durability of third-generation EGFR-TKIs in LUAD (Fig. 7).

To quantify cellular apoptosis following designated treatments, an Annexin V-FITC/PI Apoptosis Detection Kit (KeygenBioTECH) was employed in strict accordance with the manufacturer’s instructions.
